Where a county deed is filed

A deed for a house in St. Louis County goes to the Recorder of Deeds in Clayton, but only when the parcel lies outside the City of St. Louis. The counter is at 41 South Central Avenue. Call (314) 615-7100. The office is open Monday through Thursday only, from 8 until 3:30.

Besides deeds, the same staff file subdivision plats, federal and state tax liens and other written instruments touching real or personal property, and they issue marriage licenses. Anything recorded there is open to public research. Written questions can go to Recorder@stlouiscountymo.gov or to 41 South Central Avenue, Clayton, MO 63105. For a sale in Florissant, Chesterfield, Ballwin or any other municipality in the county, the closing agent usually carries the signed deed to this office, so a seller seldom visits in person.

What the county charges to record a deed

The county charges $26 for page one and $3 for every page after it. A document that ignores the state layout rules draws a further $25. Anyone who files electronically may pay a vendor's own charges on top.

The layout rules come from RSMo 59.310. A recorder may turn away a paper that fails them, or accept it with the surcharge. A deed packet for this office typically needs:

  • single-sided pages on white or pale paper, loose rather than bound;
  • type of at least eight points, in black or dark ink, with legible signatures and typed names beneath them;
  • three clear inches at the top of the first sheet, reserved for the recorder's certification, and three-quarters of an inch around the other edges;
  • on that first sheet, under the margin: title, date, every grantor with marital status, every grantee, statutory addresses, and the legal description.

If you overpay, a refund check comes back only when the excess tops $10. Smaller overages go into the county's general fund.

County office versus city office

They are separate. In 1877 St. Louis voters chose to leave the county, and the two have kept separate land records ever since. A house a few blocks east or west of the boundary can therefore belong to a different office.

The city's recorder works from City Hall, Room 126, at 1200 Market Street, and publishes its own prices. Look at the parcel's address first, because a deed sent to the wrong office will not help your closing.

Mailing a deed or filing it electronically

Mailing works. Send or hand over the original notarized deed, with a check or money order made out to ROD, to the Clayton address. The county returns the original within a week of recording. Electronic filing runs through the third-party vendors listed on the county's e-recording page, and a business that wants to file that way contacts a vendor to set up service.

A seller with a single deed rarely needs that, because the title company handling the sale will normally take care of the recording and pass along a copy. If you wonder whether any charge besides recording applies to your particular deed, ask the Recorder's office at (314) 615-7100 or the closing agent before you sign.

If the recorder rejects your deed

A rejected paper goes back to whoever brought it, with the reason written out. Once the problem is fixed, you can present it again. The same law lets a non-conforming paper be recorded for the $25 add-on instead of being refused.

Some papers are exempt from the layout rules and may still be recorded. The list includes documents signed before January 1, 2002, papers executed outside the United States, certified copies, and anything where an original party has died or is otherwise incapacitated. An heir selling a parent's house could fall into that last group, so tell the title company early.

Hold on to the stamped copy afterward. The top three inches carry the recorder's certification, which makes the copy your proof that the deed reached the record.

Ordering a copy or searching old deeds

You can order a certified copy online from the county's vendor, or go in person. The counter takes cards only. Pages cost $2 for the first and $1 for each after, a typical printed deed comes to $5 plus a convenience charge, and each certification adds $1.

  • The web search reaches recorded deeds through 1974.
  • If you bought before 1974, book an appointment for a deed search in Clayton.
  • You may also book one if you would rather search on site.
  • State law caps what a recorder may charge for a paper copy of a recorded instrument at $2 for the first page and $1 for each later page, which matches the county's copy price.

Pull a recent copy before you list. The buyer's title company will check names and the legal description against it.

The county in brief

St. Louis County lies in eastern Missouri, with the Missouri River along its north edge, the Meramec River along most of the south, and the Mississippi and the City of St. Louis to the east. It has about 990,911 residents on 507.88 square miles of land, and 448,637 homes. Owners live in 69.2% of occupied homes. The typical owned house is valued at $276,800, median household income is $82,936, and median monthly rent is $1,209.

Eighty-seven municipal governments operate in the county, and roughly one resident in three lives in an unincorporated area where the county itself handles zoning and code enforcement. A deed for a house in Clayton and one for a house in Wildwood are filed at the same counter, though each municipality governs its own streets. Ask city hall about local steps before you list.

Steps for a seller

  1. Confirm your parcel is in the county and not the city.
  2. Pull a recent copy of your deed so you can compare names and the legal description with the sale contract.
  3. Let the title company prepare the new deed, or check the layout rules above if you prepare your own.
  4. Plan any in-person trip for Monday through Thursday, before 3:30.
  5. After recording, keep the stamped copy.

A sale to a cash buyer goes through the same recording steps, so the same fees and layout rules apply. The difference is speed: with no lender involved, the deed can often be signed and sent to Clayton sooner after the closing date is set.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I find the St. Louis County recorder?

At 41 South Central Avenue in Clayton, MO 63105. Call (314) 615-7100 or write to Recorder@stlouiscountymo.gov. The doors are open Monday to Thursday from 8 to 3:30.

What is the recording charge for a deed here?

Twenty-six dollars for the first page and three for each page that follows, with a $25 add-on for a paper that breaks the Missouri format rules. Vendors who handle e-recording can charge extra.

Will the county take a deed by post?

Yes. Mail the original notarized deed and a check or money order payable to ROD to the Clayton office. The county returns the original within a week of recording.

My house is in St. Louis city. Do I file in Clayton?

No. The City of St. Louis keeps its own land records at City Hall, Room 126, and charges its own prices. Clayton handles only parcels in the county.

How far back does the online deed search go?

Recorded deeds can be searched through 1974. A property bought before that year calls for an appointment at the Clayton office.

Where the Jackson County Recorder of Deeds is

Only one recording counter exists, in the Historic Truman Courthouse at 112 W. Lexington, Suite 30, Independence, MO 64050. Walk-ins are served weekdays between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m., except county holidays. Reach the staff at 816-881-4483 or records@jacksongov.org.

The Kansas City courthouse at 415 E. 12th St. takes tax payments, but the recorder is located only in Independence. Mail submissions go to the same suite. Banks, title companies and law offices often file electronically instead, and electronic signatures and notarization are accepted that way as well as at the counter and by mail.

What the recorder does in a house sale

Staff review each paper, index it and confirm it meets the minimum recording requirements before it joins the public record. They will not fill in a form, coach you through one or judge what it says. For wording, hire a title agent or Missouri attorney.

The buyer's deed is indexed here, and so is the lender's release once a loan is paid off. Nearly 100 kinds of documents are recorded, among them:

  • Deeds and deeds of trust
  • Releases and assignments of mortgages
  • Uniform Commercial Code real estate filings
  • State and federal tax liens and releases
  • Notices of mechanic's lien
  • Plats and surveys

Page one of a standard deed is $23, and every page after is $3. This schedule governs every document received on or after August 28, 2026, by e-recording or mail, whatever the postmark.

Where the money goes

The $23 first-page charge breaks down as $8 for the state and $15 for the county. State money is divided among four funds: Local Preservation, State Surveyor, State Housing Trust and the State Statutory County Recorder's Fund. County money feeds the General Fund, the Recorder's Fee Fund, a County Homeless Fund and a Technology Fund. All $3 for each further page lands in the county General Fund.

On a settlement statement the recording line is a flat sum set by page count, so a deed with exhibits costs a few dollars more.

Ways to pay

Mailed checks go to the Recorder of Deeds Department. At the counter the office takes cash, checks and cards. Cards carry a 2.75% merchant processing fee on the whole transaction, which makes a big batch of documents noticeably dearer by card than by check.

Certified copies of deeds can be ordered online through the county's Aumentum portal at aumentumweb.jacksongov.org. Certified marriage license copies are $10, payable by personal check or money order if you ask by mail.

What a deed must look like to be recorded

Below a three-inch blank top margin, page one lists the title, date, each grantor with marital status, each grantee, statutory addresses and the legal description. That follows Missouri statute 59.310, which also wants three-quarters of an inch at the other edges, dark ink, type of eight points or larger and light paper of twenty-pound weight or more.

  • Print on a single side, with no permanent binding.
  • Sign in dark ink and put the typed or printed name below.
  • Under the statute, a paper that misses the rules may still be recorded for $25 more.
  • Rejected papers come back with an explanation.

The county recommends leaving out nonessential personal information and publishes a page on redacting it.

Does every Kansas City address record in Jackson County?

Not always. Kansas City is a co-seat, but its limits stretch into Platte and Clay counties and a sliver of Cass. A parcel north of the Missouri River may belong to another county's recorder, so read the county named on your tax bill before you send a deed here.

Within Jackson County, the Independence office handles Lee's Summit, Blue Springs, Raytown, Grandview, Grain Valley, Oak Grove, Lone Jack and the rest. One office takes all that volume, so a complete packet with the first-page details already in place is less likely to bounce.

In an estate sale or a trust deed, the recorder looks only at format. Settle who has authority to sign with the attorney or title agent before the packet goes out, and ask whether your title company e-files.

Who files and how the sale unfolds

On a typical sale the closing agent prepares the deed and the lender's deed of trust, collects the recording fees from the funds at the table and submits both. The recorder indexes the deed in the buyer's name, and when your own loan was paid off, the lender's release is recorded the same way. You can read the result in the county's document search once it posts.

If you are a private seller handling the paperwork without a title company, you take on every step: format check, legal description, fee, delivery. Staff cannot help you draft anything, so many private sellers pay a Missouri attorney for a short review. Whichever route you pick, keep a certified copy of the recorded deed, ordered through the Aumentum portal, with your closing papers.

Preparing your packet

Gather the signed deed, the legal description and a payment sized to the page count before you send anything. A deed with a $23 first page and several exhibits can cost a few dollars more than you expect, and a card adds 2.75% to the total. If you mail the packet, send it to Suite 30 at the Truman Courthouse and expect a rejected paper to come back with a written explanation. If your title company e-records, you skip the trip and the mail time altogether.

Guarding against deed fraud

Through propertyfraudalert.com, which the recorder links, owners can sign up to be told whenever a paper is recorded against their property. A seller keeping other parcels, or an heir watching an inherited home, can use it to catch a forged deed.

The recorder's page also links a document search for county records, and certified copies of anything found there are ordered through the Aumentum portal.

Loose ends before closing

Taxes are the usual one. Because an unpaid real estate balance follows the parcel to the buyer, ask the title agent to confirm what is owed before the deed is filed. Recording a military discharge here costs nothing, and a copy request needs a notarized form.

Once the sale closes, phone Assessment so the owner and mailing address are updated. Our Jackson County property tax guide covers the bill, deadlines and appeals. When an inherited or tenant-occupied house complicates the paperwork, a cash buyer's closing agent can do the same recording and pay the fees at the table.

How much does Jackson County charge to record a deed?

Page one is $23 and each later page is $3 for documents received on or after August 28, 2026. A card payment adds 2.75% to the whole transaction.

Can I record a deed in Kansas City?

No, recording is done only in Independence, at 112 W. Lexington, Suite 30. You can also mail the packet, and title companies can e-record.

Will the recorder prepare my deed?

No. Staff index and review papers but do not complete forms. Ask a title agent or Missouri attorney to draft yours.

What if my deed breaks the format rules?

It may be returned with a reason, or recorded for $25 more under Missouri statute 59.310. Correct the margins, type size and first-page details first to avoid both.

Where can I order a certified deed copy?

Use the county's Aumentum portal, aumentumweb.jacksongov.org. Certification is $1, plus $2 for the first copied page and $1 for each more.

What the Boone County Recorder of Deeds does

This office keeps the public record of land transactions in the county and also issues marriage licenses. Deeds, deeds of trust, releases, easements, plats, surveys, restrictions, cemetery deeds, wills, road rights of way and affidavits all end up in its indexes. If you're selling in Columbia, Ashland, Centralia or anywhere else in the county, the closing isn't finished until the deed reaches this office.

The deed and deed of trust index reaches back to 1821, and computerized real estate records start in 1975. Releases and assignments have a separate index. State and federal tax liens are indexed by taxpayer name, with computerized lien records starting in 1985, and marriage records on computer begin in 1973. The office phone is 573-886-4345.

Copies of every deed and deed of trust go to the Assessor, so the recorded document is what updates ownership for the next tax bill.

Recording fees

A standard real estate document costs $26.00 for the first page and $3.00 for each page after that. Pay the amount the Recorder posts, and call 573-886-4345 if a closing agent quotes something different. Statutory authority for recorder fees is RSMo 59.310.

Card payments and overpayments

Card users pay a $1.55 fee on transactions up to $66.00 and 2.35 percent on anything larger. Those charges sit on top of the recording fee.

The Recorder keeps an overpayment of up to $10.00. The reason is speed: documents can be recorded in priority order without being bounced for a small shortfall, as long as the payment isn't below the statutory fee. Anything beyond that is receipted and deposited. To get an overpayment back, send a written request that reaches the office within 30 days of recording, and the Recorder then has 30 days to decide. UCC fixture filings are the exception, since overpayments on those are never refunded.

What a deed must include to be recorded

The Recorder's requirements follow the format rules in state law. A document that follows them records as standard. One that doesn't still records, but as a non-standard document, and a $25.00 penalty is added to the normal fee under RSMo 59.310.

  • Title and date of the document on the first page, below a blank 3-inch top margin.
  • Names of every grantor with marital status, plus the grantees, on the first page.
  • Grantee mailing address and the legal description of the land on the first page.
  • Grantor signature, with the name typed or printed under each signature.
  • Notary acknowledgment with signature and seal, stamped in blank space rather than over text.
  • Letter-size paper, margins of at least three-quarters of an inch elsewhere, and type no smaller than 8 point.

A recording certificate is stamped in the top margin when the document is accepted. A rejected document comes back with a written reason. Documents signed before 2002, military separation papers, papers signed abroad, certified copies, documents where a party has died and court-formatted judgments are exempt from the layout rules.

Closing papers with special rules

A few document types ask for extra items, and they matter when a seller is paying off a loan or buying out of foreclosure.

  • A release deed must list the book and page of the deed of trust being released. If that deed of trust was recorded before January 1, 1986, the original note, marked paid, has to come along, or an affidavit of lost note from the maker and holder.
  • A trustee's deed after foreclosure must show the book and page of the foreclosed deed of trust, and the original identified note is required when that deed of trust was recorded before 1986.
  • An assignment of deed of trust should list the book and page of the instrument being assigned.
  • Fixture filings under the Uniform Commercial Code stay with the county, while other UCC filings go to the Secretary of State.

The Recorder doesn't draft deeds or answer legal questions. A title company or attorney handles preparation, and the Recorder's office handles filing and retrieval.

Seller checklist before a deed goes to the Recorder

Most recording problems come from small gaps that a closing agent can catch in advance. A few minutes of review saves the $25.00 non-standard charge and avoids a returned document.

  • Confirm every grantor name matches the prior deed and that marital status is stated.
  • Check that the legal description is on page one, or that page one points to the page where it appears.
  • Leave the top three inches clear and keep notary seals out of the margins.
  • Ask whether a lien, such as a state or federal tax lien indexed by taxpayer name, will need a discharge recorded at $7.50.
  • Request a certified or plain copy afterward, at $1.00 per page plus $1.00 for the certification.

The same counter handles marriage licenses, at $53.00, but that has nothing to do with a house sale.

How recording affects the Boone County tax bill

Because the Recorder passes every deed to the Assessor, the date a deed is recorded can decide whose name appears on the next tax bill. A closing on or after October 1 may produce a bill in the seller's name at the old address unless the buyer reports the sale. Ask the title company to confirm the deed was recorded, then tell the Collector or Assessor about the new owner.

Fees collected here go to the County Treasurer, apart from special fees forwarded directly to the state each month. The Recorder also files a monthly fee report with the Auditor and settles up yearly with the County Commission.

Boone County market and deed volume

Boone County has 84,371 housing units for 2025, and owner-occupied homes have a median value of $272,800. Owners live in 57.7 percent of homes, median gross rent is $1,088, and 787 building permits were issued in 2025.

That adds up to a steady flow of filings: sales, refinances, releases after payoffs and new subdivision plats. Columbia, with the University of Missouri, anchors most of that activity, and the separate plat and survey fees reflect the platting that growth brings. A cash sale records the same way as a financed one, minus the new deed of trust.

Frequently asked questions

How much does the Boone County Recorder charge for a standard deed?

$26.00 for the first page and $3.00 for each added page. A non-standard document costs $51.00 for the first page.

What happens if my deed is not in standard format?

It is recorded as non-standard, and a $25.00 penalty is added to the regular fee under RSMo 59.310. Following the margin, signature and notary rules avoids that charge.

Can I get an overpayment refunded?

Only in some cases. The Recorder keeps overpayments up to $10.00, and larger ones can be requested back in writing within 30 days of recording. UCC fixture filing overpayments are not refunded.

Does the Recorder prepare deeds for homeowners?

No. The office files and indexes documents and helps people search records, but legal drafting belongs to an attorney or title company.

How far back do Boone County land records go?

The general index reaches back to 1821, and computerized real estate records begin in 1975. Call 573-886-4345 for help with older books.

What makes a deed non-standard?

Missing the Recorders Association of Missouri layout rules adds a $25 charge, which is the gap between $26 and $51 on page one. The rules date from January 1, 2002, and a title company or attorney will normally build them into the deed form. A seller drafting a deed alone should check each item.

Page one must show the title, the date, each grantor with marital status, each grantee, statutory addresses and the legal description. Several kinds of paper are exempt and pay only the per-page fee. Documents signed before January 1, 2002 are one group. A document is also exempt when one of the original parties has died or is incapacitated.

A cover sheet is optional, but one that is used is recorded as page one and must have the 3-inch top margin and the first-page information. A paper sent in for re-recording needs a new first page or cover sheet meeting the same rules. Rejected documents come back with a reason stated.

Property tax is a separate matter. The Platte County Collector bills it, with statements due on receipt and delinquent after December 31. The Assessor's office also lists a sales validation and education coordinator at (816) 858-1256, a useful number when a sale price needs to be explained to the county.

Platte County is part of the Kansas City metro area. The July 2025 estimate is 114,400 residents and 47,969 housing units. A typical owned home is worth $345,100, owners occupy 67.4 percent of homes and 425 building permits were issued in 2025. The county was organized on December 31, 1838, and the Platte City courthouse carries a National Register listing. Because new documents are accepted only until 4 p.m., send a deed early in the day.

From deed to recorded record, step by step

  3. Call (816) 858-3326 for the exact total, since overpayments are not refunded.

Bring it between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. on a weekday. The office stays open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. for searches and copies.

Register for a free account at plattemo.icounty.com and set your criteria in the Record Notification Service. The system emails you when a matching deed reaches the office.

Staff do not decide what should be recorded. They check a document against state requirements and then keep it forever as a public record.

When a mortgage is paid off, a release of the deed of trust gets recorded. That release does not prove you own the house. The deed from your seller does. Deed Watch, a free email alert at deedwatch.com, will message you whenever a document is recorded under a name you pick.

Where to take a deed in Greene County

The Assessor's Public Access website lists a parcel's owner, taxing district and school district and refreshes nightly, so a recent purchase may already appear.

Documents the office files

Property records for the whole county live here, from deeds and mortgages to releases and anything else that affects title. RSMo 442.380 directs that a conveyance be recorded in the county where the real estate lies, which sends your deed to this counter.

The office has three other jobs:

  • Issuing and maintaining marriage licenses
  • Filing federal and state tax liens
  • Keeping military discharge records, with a request form and regulations posted online

Drafting is not on the list. Staff will not write your deed, so hire a title company or lawyer for that.

Recording fees

The posted schedule charges $26.00 for page one of a real estate document and $3.00 for each page after that. If you want the original returned by mail, enclose a stamped return envelope or add postage to your payment.

Greene County recording charges
Document or serviceCharge

Same, each page after the first$3.00

Senate Bill 938 adds $2 to the charge for real estate documents, plats and surveys, so phone the office for the current total. The state's own piece is set in RSMo 59.319: a six dollar user fee on every recorded instrument, on top of whatever else the office charges.

What makes a deed fit to record

Under RSMo 59.310 the recorder may refuse a paper that breaks the layout rules, or take it for an extra $25. Treat the list as a checklist for your title company:

  • Single-sided, unbound pages in dark ink, with type of at least eight points, on light paper of twenty-pound weight or more
  • A blank three-inch band across the top of page one for the recorder's certification, and three-quarter inch margins on all sides
  • Under the blank band: title, date, grantors with marital status, grantees, statutory addresses and the legal description

RSMo 59.330 adds two demands. The deed needs a legal description, and unless it is an easement or right-of-way it must give a mailing address for one of the grantees. A refused paper goes back to whoever presented it, with the reason in writing.

Packing a deed for the counter

Before you drive to Springfield, run through this list. Is the legal description copied exactly from the vesting deed? Is there a mailing address for at least one grantee, unless the paper is an easement or right-of-way? Do the margins and ink match the rules above? Is the fee worked out from the page count, with a stamped return envelope or postage added if you want the original mailed back?

A single missed item sends the paper back, and the office will not fix it for you. Staff cannot draft or edit a deed, so questions about wording belong with a title company or attorney. Ask them to read the packet once more the day before, and keep your own copy of everything you hand over.

If you inherited the house or have tenants in it, say so early, since the order of recording can matter. A cash buyer's closing agent handles the same recording steps and pays the fees from the closing funds.

The index does not work from street addresses. It answers to a full legal description, a book and page, a name or a document number. With only an address in hand, ask the Assessor for the legal description first.

The law bars the recorder from running lien searches, and liens are filed in places besides this office. Staff will still help you page through the records. A subscription service lets you download raw data, though it does not show images online. For a Greene County sale, rely on the title company's full search.

Copies of recorded papers

Recorded documents are $1.00 a page to copy, certification is another $1.00, and a plat copy is $5.00. Certified marriage license copies are $9.00, and by mail they require a cashier's check or money order since personal checks are refused.

Bring or send whatever the index needs. A legal description, book and page, name or document number will find the instrument, and the fee is counted by page.

How recording closes out a home sale

Recording comes last. Once you close, the signed deed travels to 940 N Boonville Ave to be entered in the county record. The Assessor then updates its tax maps from the warranty deeds the recorder sends over, which is why lot lines and owner names in the county's parcel data follow your deed.

Several days ahead of signing, have your closing agent proofread the legal description, the grantee's mailing address and the margins.

It has 142,405 housing units, and owners live in 57.5 percent of homes. The median owned home is valued at $221,300 and median gross rent is $989. The county issued 966 building permits in 2025, so recordings come steadily from new construction and resales alike.

Does Greene County charge transfer tax on a deed?

The fee schedule shows none, and the recorder's FAQ says the selling price need not appear on a recorded deed. Page-based recording charges apply. Ask the title company about other closing costs.

What is the cutoff time to record a deed in Greene County?

4:00 PM on a business day. Papers presented later are recorded starting at 8:00 AM the next business day.

Will the Greene County recorder tell me about liens on my house?

No. The law bars the office from running lien searches, and liens may be filed elsewhere. A title company's search is the reliable check before closing.

From the Assessor, Room 35 at 940 N Boonville Ave, or its Public Access website. The recorder cannot search by street address.

It comes back to you with the reason. A paper that misses the layout rules in RSMo 59.310 can instead be recorded for an extra $25.

Anything handed over after 3:30 pm waits until the next business day. With a late-afternoon closing, find out from the title company when the deed actually gets to Troy, because that decides the recording date.

Clerks check each paper against the recording statutes and stop there. Legal advice, title or lien searches, typing up a deed, blank forms, ownership disputes and notary work are all outside what they do. Take those to an attorney or your title agent. If you visit in person, bring your closing paperwork, and phone ahead when you are unsure whether a document counts as standard or non-standard, since the fee differs.

This office is the county's home for land records and marriage licenses. Common filings include deeds, deeds of trust, releases, easements, surveys, plats, restrictions, wills, affidavits, patents and road rights of way. Servicemen's records are kept here too, and a tax lien goes on file when requested.

Filing is not a formality. RSMo 442.380: any written paper that transfers land goes to the recorder in the county where that land lies. RSMo 442.400: a deed that is never filed holds up only against the signers and people who knew about it. A buyer in that spot can face later claims, so get the deed to Troy within days of signing.

What does Lincoln County charge to record a deed?

Expect $26.00 for page one of a standard real estate document, then $3.00 per added page. Senate Bill 938 added $2.00 to the first-page fee, and $26.00 is the number to budget.

  • Keep three-quarters of an inch of white space down both sides and along the bottom.
  • A legible legal description of the parcel.
  • A proper notarization, with the notary's signature legible and the seal placed legibly beneath it.
  • No handwritten documents.
  • Print in dark ink on light paper, with letters no smaller than eight-point.

The same section allows a recorder to take a nonconforming paper for an extra $25. Some papers are exempt, for example those signed before January 1, 2002 or executed outside the United States.   1. Get the deed prepared by an attorney or title company, because the recorder will not type one.
  2. Sign in front of a notary and make sure the signature and seal can be read.
  3. Look over page one for the 3 inch blank top and the legal description.
  4. Pay the recording fee: $26.00 for page one, $3.00 for each page after.
  5. Get it to Troy before 3:30 pm for same-day recording.
  6. Check with the Assessor's office that ownership was updated.

Title companies do all of this routinely. Selling an inherited house? A small estate affidavit and certificate can be recorded to show the heirs hold title, so hand the probate papers to your closing agent early.

A little prep helps. Learn who will carry the deed to the counter and when, ask for the exact recording charge so it lands on the settlement statement, and save the recorded copy when it returns. Page one of a standard real estate document is $26.00, and every page after it is $3.00. A document the county classes as non-standard starts at $49.00 for page one.

No. The office reviews documents for recording requirements and does not draft deeds, hand out forms or search title. Hire a lawyer or a title agent.

What time must I deliver a document for same-day recording?

Before 3:30 pm. Anything presented later is recorded on the following business day.

Do I have to record a deed after selling my Lincoln County house?

Yes. State law sends every land conveyance to the recorder where the parcel sits, and an unrecorded deed binds only the parties and anyone with actual notice. Your closing agent normally files it.

Assessor field crews gather data in marked vehicles, wear safety vests with body cameras and county ID, and knock first. Staff log each item, index it and keep it for good: deeds and deeds of trust, release deeds, plats and surveys, powers of attorney, deed restrictions, federal and state tax liens, and UCC fixture filings. You can also get a marriage license there, and a veteran's discharge papers are filed at no charge.

Recording is the buyer's shield. RSMo 442.400 makes an unrecorded instrument valid just between the signers and people with actual notice of it. If the deed sits unfiled, outsiders can ignore it.

Where to file and how

The counter is at 102 E. Wall St., Harrisonville, MO 64701, open weekdays 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Call 816-380-8118 with questions. Drafting is not part of the job here, so hire a title company or real estate attorney to prepare the paperwork.

  • Bring it in or mail it to Wall Street, with the correct fee enclosed.
  • E-record through iCounty. First sign a registration packet, then mail it to Wall Street or email it to the address on the county's e-recording page. Payment is by ACH inside the portal.
  • ACH payment is refused for documents in delinquent status.
  • Registered users can search the document index online at no cost.

A free fraud alert system lives at casscounty.com/fraud. Enroll a personal or business name and you are told whenever a document carrying it is recorded.

Recording fees

The price of recording mixes state statute with a county formatting rule. RSMo 59.310 sets the base per-page charge, and RSMo 59.319 adds a flat user fee on each recorded instrument. The county's fee page carries the current posted schedule, so look there before writing a check.

Deed formatting rules

Formatting standards have applied since January 1, 2002. The exceptions are documents signed earlier, military separation papers, documents executed outside the United States, certified copies, documents where an original party has died or is incapacitated, court-formatted judgments and national-form UCC fixture filings.

  • Letter-size sheets (8.5 by 11 inches), white or light, 20 pound stock or heavier, one side only, in dark ink with at least 8 point type.
  • Leave 3 inches blank at the top of page one for the Recorder's stamp, and keep at least three quarters of an inch clear on all other edges.
  • Sign in dark ink and put the name typed, printed or stamped under each signature.
  • Under that blank band on page one, show the title, date, grantors with marital status, grantees, any statutory addresses and the legal description.
  • Parties tagged with the words Grantor or Grantee so they can be indexed. The person filing adds those tags, not the office.

A cover page is optional, but it must carry the same top margin and first-page details. Re-recording a document calls for a new cover sheet, fresh signatures and a new notarization.

Why documents get rejected

When the office turns a document down, the reason comes back in writing. Its FAQ names the common causes, and most are easy to catch before you file.

  • The fee is wrong.
  • Page one lacks the required designations.
  • Text runs into the margins.
  • A signature has no typed name or no acknowledgment.
  • Anything affecting land needs a real legal description, and a street address won't pass.
  • The grantee's mailing address is missing from a land transfer.
  • The copy is too faint to reproduce.
  • A release or assignment cites several book and page numbers without the extra $5 each.

Blanket assignments are not accepted. A rejection can cost days, which is why many sellers let the title company do the filing.

Turnaround and what the public can see

Expect real estate recordings back the same day or in 24 hours, weekends and holidays excluded. The originals return to the submitter, often a lender or servicer. When a mortgage is paid off, the lender typically files a short release deed. A buyer ordinarily gets the deed to the new house at closing.

Some things the office won't do. No sale price appears on recorded real estate documents. Staff won't phone with book, page or recording time, and state law keeps them from searching for liens. Since liens may also sit with the court or the Collector, your title insurer, lender or agent is the better source. Public computers at the Harrisonville office let anyone view a recorded instrument.

Property tax when a house sells

Real estate tax is billed by the Collector of Revenue at 2725 Cantrell Road, Harrisonville, phone 816-380-8377, weekdays 8 to 4:30. November brings the statement, December 31 is the deadline, and mail is judged by U.S. postmark. A delinquent balance can pick up penalties of up to 25 percent in year one.

  • The tax lien rides with the land, which makes a new owner liable for any back taxes.
  • Closing generally prorates the year's tax between buyer and seller, and the Collector is paid nothing at the sale.
  • Until the Collector or Assessor hears about the new owner, a bill can still be mailed to the seller. If you get one, forward the buyer's name and address to the Collector.
  • Homes are assessed at 19 percent of market value, commercial parcels at 32 and farmland at 12.
  • Unpaid land goes to the yearly tax sale on August's fourth Monday at 10 a.m. Next up: Monday, August 23, 2027.

Values come from the Assessor. Levies are voted by school, fire, library and hospital boards, and the Collector has no say in them.

Cass County housing context

Greater Kansas City reaches into Cass County, though the courthouse is in Harrisonville. The county grew from 107,824 residents in 2020 to 115,859 by mid-2025. Of 48,259 housing units, 75.6 percent are owner-occupied, with a middle home value of $292,400 and median rent of $1,205. A house in Belton, Raymore, Peculiar, Pleasant Hill or Garden City is still filed at the Harrisonville office.

Frequently asked questions

What do deed recording fees run?

Page one costs $5 and each added page $3, plus a $6 user fee per instrument. Instruments listed in RSMo 59.330 add a $3 housing trust fund fee, and a badly formatted document adds $25. Look at the posted schedule before paying.

Can the Recorder write or fix my deed?

No. Staff review and file documents but never draft or alter them, and they send people to a title company or attorney. A flawed deed is corrected through a corrective filing or a re-recording with a new cover sheet, signatures and acknowledgment.

How long does recording take?

Real estate recordings come back the same day or within 24 hours, not counting weekends and holidays. Registered iCounty users can see results in minutes. A rejected paper filing restarts the clock, so check margins and page-one items first.

Can I record a deed electronically?

Yes, after registering. Fill out the e-recording packet through the Recorder or iCounty and return it by mail to Wall Street or by email. You can pay by ACH in the portal, though ACH is refused for delinquent documents.

Will the Recorder tell me what a house sold for?

No. The price is not on recorded documents, and nobody at the office gives closing details by phone. Ask your title insurer, lender or agent. The public computers display the deed, its book and page and the date recorded.

What the recorder keeps on file

This office holds the permanent record of who owns land in Newton County. It records warranty deeds, deeds of trust, releases, plats, surveys and powers of attorney, and it keeps military discharges along with state and federal tax liens.

A few limits to know before you call:

  • Staff cannot practice law, so they will not draft a deed, supply legal forms or explain what a filed paper means.
  • The office does not produce abstracts of title or opinions on the status of a title (RSMo 59.200.1).

What a deed must look like before it is accepted

The recorder may reject a paper that fails the layout test in RSMo 59.310, or record it and add a $25 penalty. The office's format page spells out what passes.

Indexing relies on labels. The words grantor and grantee must sit beside the parties, and a house's street address cannot replace a legal description. Checking a title problem

This counter cannot clear a title. It is the place to confirm that a deed of trust has a recorded release, that a plat or survey for the parcel is on file, and that a tax lien has been filed or released. Releases and assignments must cite the book and page of the paper they refer to.

For anything beyond that, such as who holds a valid claim, bring in an attorney or a title searcher. Sellers of an inherited or tenant-occupied house often begin with a title search to learn which recorded papers need a release before a buyer can close. A delinquent tax sale also runs each August, so a parcel with unpaid taxes can carry extra recorded history.

Courthouse offices and the tax bill

Several county offices share the courthouse, so one trip can cover them all. Ask each for current figures.

  • The county clerk, (417) 451-8221, can tell you where a valuation appeal is filed. The Board of Equalization is among the boards the commission appoints.

A tax obligation is fixed on January 1, the law gives no pro-rating, and the current owner is responsible for taxes due. Ask your closing office how the year's bill is split on the settlement sheet, and ask the collector what is still unpaid before you sign. Where the land records are kept

The Recorder's staff work from Suite 100 on the ground level of the courthouse annex, 1 West Liberty Street, Farmington. The county suggests using the rear main parking lot entrance. The office records, maintains and archives deeds, liens, marriage licenses, surveys, plats and military discharge papers.

  • Phone: 573-756-2323, or 573-431-6505 then option 1 and 7.
  • Hours: weekdays, 8:00 a.m. until 4:00 p.m.
  • Cards: debit and credit are taken, with a convenience fee of at least $2.00 on each transaction.
  • Search: the deed index books and all recorded documents are online in Tapestry under Land Records Search. A Laredo subscription is another option, so ask the office.

This office also records federal and state tax liens and their releases, and you can ask for copies by letter or at the counter. Down the hall are the Assessor (Suite 200) and the Collector (Suite 201), which makes a single visit enough for a lien check, a parcel record and a tax payoff ahead of a sale.

Recording fees come from RSMo 59.310. Senate Bill 938 added a flat $2.00 statewide increase for documents, marriage licenses and plats or surveys. Call for the all-in total for your page count before you drive over.

If you wonder whether a transfer-related charge applies to your deed, ask the Recorder at 573-756-2323.

Formatting rules for a deed

RSMo 59.310 lets the Recorder refuse a paper that ignores the layout rules, or accept it with a $25 surcharge. If it is refused, the reason must be given in writing. Even certified court copies must include the property's legal description.

  • Paper: letter size, white or pale, 20 pound stock, printed on one side, with no attachments stapled on unless a statute demands them.
  • Margins: three blank inches across the top of page one for the Recorder, and at least 3/4 inch elsewhere.
  • Type: eight point or larger, in black or dark ink, sharp enough to copy cleanly.
  • Signatures: dark ink, each with the signer's name typed, printed or stamped below.

Under that margin the first page lists the title, the date, every grantor (labeled Grantor, with marital status), every grantee (labeled Grantee), any addresses a statute requires, the legal description and book and page references if they apply. A cover sheet can hold the same details. Some papers skip the format rules altogether: anything signed before January 1, 2002, military separation papers, documents executed outside the United States and court judgments.

What if a recorded deed has an error?

It can be re-recorded, but the second filing faces the same tests as a fresh one. The county wants correct margins, legibility and first page information, a new cover sheet saying why the document is being recorded again, and a new acknowledgment from the notary.

With a closing around the corner, a mistake can hold up the title company. It takes only a wrong legal description or a grantor's name left off. Ask the escrow officer to check the deed before signing. Owners can also sign up for the Recorder's free Property Fraud Alert, which sends a warning if someone records a fake document claiming your home. Subscribe online or phone 800-728-3858.

The county around Farmington

St. Francois County is part of Missouri's Lead Belt, with Farmington as seat and biggest city. It counts roughly 67,809 residents in 29,596 homes, and owners hold 68.2% of households. Median home value is $169,300, median rent $794 and median household income $57,477. Five school districts serve it: Bismarck R-V, Farmington R-VII, North St. Francois County R-1, St. Francois County Central R-III and West St. Francois County R-IV.

Property tax, tax sale and installment plan

Suite 201 houses the Collector (573-756-2645), who handles both current and past-due tax and holds the county tax sale on the fourth Monday of August. Parcels still owing after June 30 can be redeemed only by paying in full with cash, a money order or a cashier's check, up to 4:00 p.m. on the Friday before the sale. The Assessor's number is 573-756-1878, in Suite 200.

Pay at the Collector's office or online. December 31 is the last day each year to pay without late charges. Owners whose taxes are not paid through a mortgage escrow can use an installment plan run with EquaPay. The county describes four steps: look up your bill, create an account and pick a draft date and method (bank account or card), let EquaPay calculate payments from the time left before the due date, and finish enrollment so it pays the county on time.

Senior tax credit and your buyer

A senior tax credit belongs to the qualifying taxpayer's homestead and cannot be handed to the next owner or carried to another house. Someone who moves and still qualifies applies again, and the new address gets its own base year.

Enrollment runs March 1 through May 31, in person at the Collector's office between 9:00 a.m. and 3:00 p.m., with photo ID. Applicants must be 62 by January 1 of the base year and current on tax. Review can take up to 30 days, and both spouses on the deed are asked to apply in person. Trust or LLC owners must bring their documents.

The credit equals the difference between this year's tax on the homestead and the base-year tax. Assessed value is not frozen, so the credit can change, and by law the State Blind Pension Fund and voter-approved bond levies stay outside it. Delinquent tax disqualifies an applicant. If you are selling, expect the buyer's first bill to differ from yours, and ask the Collector (573-756-2645) what applies to the parcel.

Recording a deed when you sell

Typically the title company or closing attorney drafts the deed, gets it signed and notarized, and files it with the Recorder once the sale closes. You should read the legal description and both parties' names before signing, because a typo there often leads to a second filing. Hang on to the stamped copy as evidence the deed made it onto the record.

A cash sale goes the same way. You skip the wait for a buyer's loan, yet the deed meets identical format rules and fees, so find out from the closing agent who pays them.

Frequently asked questions

How do I search for a recorded deed?

Use the Land Records Search tab on the Recorder's page, which opens Tapestry and shows the deed index books and recorded documents. You can also call 573-756-2323 or visit the annex in Farmington.

When can I visit the Recorder?

The doors are open Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Holiday closings are posted on the county website's office closures page.

Why might my deed come back unrecorded?

The usual causes are a missing legal description, a first page without the three-inch top margin, text smaller than eight point or missing grantor and grantee labels. The office must return a rejected document with the reason.

Does the Recorder accept cards?

Yes. The office takes debit and credit cards and charges a minimum $2.00 convenience fee on every transaction.

Is property tax paid to the Recorder?

No. The Collector bills and collects property tax at Suite 201 of the same annex building. The Recorder handles deeds, liens and plats.

Property taxes are separate

Recording a deed does not touch the tax bill. The Franklin County Collector works from Room 103 at 400 E Locust in Union and can be reached at 636-583-6353. One statement from that office may cover the county and 64 other taxing entities.

Tax is due by December 31. Afterward it is delinquent, and RSMo 140.100 adds an 18 percent penalty on the year's delinquency. Delinquent land goes up for sale on the fourth Monday in August (RSMo 140.150), and owners can pay right up to the sale.

Buyers get one shortcut. If you purchase fewer than 30 days after the county mailed the statement, you may take an assessment appeal directly to the State Tax Commission. In all other cases the Board of Equalization goes first, and it takes filings through the second Monday in July.

Step by step after you sell

Many sales close at a title company, which can draft the deed, collect the recording fee and file the paper. In a private sale or a family transfer, you handle that yourself:

  1. Have the deed prepared to the layout rules above.
  2. Check the legal description against the vesting deed.
  3. Confirm the page count and the fee with the Recorder's office.
  4. Deliver the deed, then keep the recorded copy as your proof.

Before closing, tell the title company which tax years are open and whether a judgment, mechanic's claim or other lien is on the property. An inherited house or one with tenants may need other papers recorded first, so ask what comes ahead of the deed and what a cash buyer would pay off at the table.

Finish by giving the buyer a clear contact at the Collector and the Assessor, so the first tax bill and any value notice reach the new owner and not you. Hold on to your closing statement and the recorded deed together in one folder, since later questions about who owed what usually trace back to those two papers.

Frequently asked questions

With the county Recorder of Deeds. The county home page has a Record My Deeds link. Call for the room, hours and payment methods, or ask your title company to file.

How much is the recording fee in Franklin County?

The statute's base amount is $5 for page one and $3 for each page after. The office can quote the total for your page count.

Why did the Recorder reject my deed?

Most often a layout problem. RSMo 59.310 calls for a three-inch top margin, dark ink, type of at least eight points and the first-page details. The paper comes back with a written reason, or it can be recorded for an extra $25.

Does recording pay off property taxes?

No. Taxes are owed to the Collector at 636-583-6353 by December 31. Unpaid land can be offered at the August sale.

What area does the Franklin County Recorder serve?

The whole county, including Union, Washington, Pacific, Sullivan, New Haven, St. Clair, Berger and Gerald, plus unincorporated places such as Gray Summit and Villa Ridge.

What the Recorder of Deeds does

Land transfers and ownership changes in Jefferson County, Missouri, are kept on public record here. Staff record deeds, deeds of trust, releases, easements, plats, restrictions, surveys and affidavits, and the office also issues marriage licenses. Military discharge papers (DD214) and tax liens can be recorded on request.

  • Address: 729 Maple Street, Hillsboro, MO 63050.
  • Phone: 636-797-5414.
  • Cutoff: a document presented after 4:30 PM is processed the following business day.
  • Location rule: a document goes on record in the county where the land sits, so this office cannot record property in another county.

Drafting is outside the office's role. Employees will not write a document, supply a blank form or notarize what they record, and they send owners to a title company or real estate attorney. Bring finished, signed and notarized papers to the counter.

What a deed needs before it is accepted

Missouri's section 59.310 sets the rules, and the county posts them on its recording requirements page. Expect a refusal if your document misses one of the following.

  • Single-sided, unbound pages of white or light paper, 20 pound weight or heavier, with dark ink and type of 8 point or larger.
  • Room for the recorder's stamp: 3 inches left blank at the top of page one, and three-fourths of an inch or more on the remaining edges.
  • Below that margin on page one: the title, date, grantor names with marital status, grantee names, any statutory addresses, the legal description and any reference book and page.
  • A true legal description, such as lot, block and plat, or metes and bounds. A street address never counts.
  • A notary acknowledgment with seal and signature, plus a mailing address for at least one grantee.

The format rules can be bypassed for a $25 surcharge, which lets a noncompliant paper go on record anyway. Some categories never face the rules: documents signed before January 1, 2002, military separation papers, papers signed abroad, certified copies and court judgments.

Sellers of acreage face one more local step. A transfer deed describing under 10 acres outside any city, or only part of a subdivision lot, needs an exemption from the county Planning and Zoning Department first, or the recorder will not take it.

What it costs to record or copy a document

Lawmakers in Jefferson City set the fees, and the counter prices each document by how many pages it has. Payment comes first, by cash or by a check payable to the Jefferson County Recorder of Deeds. The county links a Real Estate Recording Fees PDF among its recorder quick links, or ask your title company what your deed will cost.

What happens after a deed reaches the office

There are six steps, which explains why a closing package can take a day or two to come back.

  1. Staff check dates, signatures, name spellings and the acknowledgment.
  2. The document is accepted and priced by page count.
  3. It receives a date and time stamp and a document number, and page one is sealed.
  4. It is scanned.
  5. It is indexed under the grantor and grantee names.
  6. A second check confirms the index entry, then the document is mailed to the address provided. Including a self-addressed envelope speeds that return.

A rejected deed goes back to the preparer with the reason. If a deed is being re-recorded, it must be acknowledged again and must say why.

Which deed fits my sale or transfer?

The recorder's FAQ describes three common kinds. With a warranty deed, a seller conveys title and promises that no liens from the seller or earlier owners cloud it. A quit claim deed lets current owners add or remove an owner, change a name or correct an error. A beneficiary deed, also called a time of death deed, records what the owner wants to happen after death.

A deed of trust is the mortgage lien. Each new loan or refinance records a new one, and when the debt is paid the lender must record a deed of release that cites the original document number. If an old lien was never released, ask the lender for that paper before closing.

The office recommends an attorney or title company for any deed, though an owner may write their own if it meets Missouri's formatting rules.

Searching Jefferson County land records

In person, the vault index lists grantors (sellers) and grantees (buyers) alphabetically. Look up your own name as grantee to find the deed from your purchase, then follow the book and page number it gives. Online there are three routes: a pay-per-search site, a Laredo subscription covering records from April 1985 to the present, and the hosted COTT Systems site for older records.

If the buyer's name draws a blank, try the seller's name too, since each recording is indexed under both parties. Write down the document number and the book and page for your files.

Laredo requires a signed user agreement from the Recorder. Losing your deed does not cost you ownership, because the recording is the main evidence of title and a certified copy can replace the original.

The recorder quick links also include a Property Fraud Alert notice. Owners of paid-off houses who get contacted about a deed transfer should read it.

The documents in a typical closing

A house sale in Jefferson County often produces three recordings back to back: a deed of release for the seller's old loan, the warranty deed to the buyer, and the buyer's new deed of trust. Each is checked, priced by page count and indexed separately, so one closing can add several entries to the grantor and grantee index.

Ask your title company which documents it plans to present and in what order. Communities whose deeds are filed here include Arnold, Festus, De Soto, Crystal City, Pevely, Herculaneum, Hillsboro and Byrnes Mill, while Eureka is mostly on the St. Louis County side.

If you sell for cash, expect fewer pieces of paper. With no buyer loan, the closing usually needs only the release of your old loan and the deed to the buyer, which also means fewer fees at the recorder's counter.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a deed in Jefferson County, Missouri?

At the Recorder of Deeds office, 729 Maple Street, Hillsboro. Phone 636-797-5414 before you go. Anything handed in after 4:30 PM is held until the next business day.

Can the recorder write my deed for me?

No. The office does not prepare documents, give legal advice, supply blank forms or notarize the papers it records. A title company or attorney handles that.

Is a street address enough for the legal description?

No. Section 59.310 calls for a lot, block and plat, or a metes and bounds or section, township and range description. An address alone is refused.

What does a certified copy of my deed cost?

The county charges $2 for the first page and $1 for each added page, plus $1 to certify. A phone order by card adds a $1 card fee and postage.

Do I need planning approval before recording a deed for a small parcel?

Sometimes. A deed for less than 10 acres in an unincorporated area, or part of a subdivision lot, needs a Planning and Zoning exemption before the recorder will take it.
